title: The aorist passive

objectives.can: Recognise aorist passive indicatives and parse them.

explanation.summary: The aorist passive has its own tense sign, -θη-, and takes the endings of an active past tense. It is the form for 'was baptized', 'was sent', 'was written', and also, for some verbs, the ordinary form for an action the subject does itself.

sections.heading: Augment, stem, -θη-, ending
body: The aorist passive is built differently from the aorist active and middle. It takes the augment, the verbal stem, the tense sign -θη-, and the endings -ν, -ς, nothing, -μεν, -τε, -σαν. From βαπτίζω: ἐβαπτίσθη is ἐ- + βαπτισ- + θη, 'he was baptized'. The plural is ἐβαπτίσθησαν. The same tense sign appears in the future passive (-θήσομαι), which you met in the lesson on the future.

In the third person singular the ending is nothing at all, so the form ends in -θη. In the third person plural it is -σαν: -θησαν. The other persons are rarer. They occur, for example, in ἐβαπτίσθητε (second person plural) and ἐβαπτίσθημεν (first person plural).

sections.heading: Changes before θ
body: A final stem consonant meets the θ of the tense sign and changes. Labial stops become φ: πέμπω gives ἐπέμφθη. Velar stops become χ: κηρύσσω gives ἐκηρύχθη, and ἄγω gives ἤχθη. Dentals become σ: ἀκούω gives ἠκούσθη, βαπτίζω gives ἐβαπτίσθη. Many stems lose their final sound or change their vowel: καλέω gives ἐκλήθη, κρίνω gives ἐκρίθη, βάλλω gives ἐβλήθη, ἐγείρω gives ἠγέρθη, and γινώσκω gives ἐγνώσθη. The present form of such a verb often cannot predict the aorist passive, so learn the pairs.
The augment works as before. The vowel lengthens (ἠκούσθη), or ἐ- is added (ἐκρίθη), or the augment stands inside a compound (ἀπεστάλη, with the prefix ἀπο-).

sections.heading: The second aorist passive
body: Some verbs form the aorist passive without θ, with the endings -ην, -ης, -η, -ημεν, -ητε, -ησαν. This is called the second aorist passive. It is the same tense and the same voice, built on the bare stem, as the second aorist is built on the bare stem in the active. The examples to learn first are ἐγράφη (γράφω, 'it was written'), ἀπεστάλη and ἀπεστάλην (ἀποστέλλω, 'he was sent', 'I was sent'), and ἐφάνη (φαίνω, 'it appeared').

sections.heading: Passive form, active sense
body: For some verbs the aorist passive is the ordinary aorist and has no passive meaning. ἀπεκρίθη is a passive form of ἀποκρίνομαι, yet it means 'he answered'. ἐπορεύθη, from πορεύομαι, means 'he went' (not 'he was gone'). ἐγενήθη, from γίνομαι, is another form of 'he became'. These are common and they have to be learned with the verb.

For other verbs, the meaning depends on the context. ἠγέρθη is a passive form of ἐγείρω; whether a translator writes 'he was raised' or 'he got up' depends on the sentence it stands in. Do not decide the meaning from the label 'passive' alone. Read the sentence, and look for an agent expressed with ὑπό and the genitive, which marks a true passive.

misunderstandings: A passive form does not always mean 'was done to'. ἀπεκρίθη and ἐπορεύθη have active meanings; the context decides.
-θη- is not an ending of a third-person form only. It stands in every person of the aorist passive: ἐβαπτίσθητε, ἐβαπτίσθημεν.

Do not mistake the aorist passive for a first aorist active because of the endings. The endings -ν, -ς, -, -μεν, -τε, -σαν of the aorist passive are the endings of a past tense, but the θη before them marks the passive.
A second aorist passive without θ (ἐγράφη) is not an active form. Look for η just before the ending and no σα.

deeper.heading: Why the passive borrows active endings
body: Historians of Greek usually explain the aorist passive as having grown out of an intransitive formation, which took the endings of the active past tenses and not the middle-passive endings of the present. This is one account of its origin, and you do not need it to read the form; it is often given as the reason why a passive form such as ἀπεκρίθη can have an active sense.

examples.analysis: ἐβαπτίσθη is aorist passive indicative, third person singular, of βαπτίζω: augment ἐ-, stem βαπτισ-, tense sign θη, no ending. The dental of the stem has become σ before θ. It is a true passive: 'he was baptized'.

examples.analysis: Six aorist passives in one verse, all third person singular. ἐφανερώθη (of φανερόω) and ἐδικαιώθη (of δικαιόω) show the plain -θη. ἐκηρύχθη shows the velar changing to χ before θ. ἐπιστεύθη is from πιστεύω. ἀνελήμφθη (of ἀναλαμβάνω) has the stem λημφ- before θ. ὤφθη is the aorist passive of ὁράω with an irregular stem; it may be translated 'he was seen' or 'he appeared'. Here the grammar needs no agent: the verse lists what was done.
